items.quote_text: The Socialist myth is that government spending creates jobs. The truth is that the only permanent job creation scheme is a healthy economy.

items.historical_context_summary: Thatcher delivered her first speech as Leader of the Conservative Party at the 1975 party conference. The UK was facing severe economic difficulties under the Labour government, including high inflation, low production, and record public spending.

items.historical_context_summary: Delivered during the 1989 Conservative Party Conference in Blackpool, against the backdrop of collapsing communist regimes in Eastern Europe. Thatcher used the speech to contrast the freedom of capitalist societies with the state control inherent in socialism.

items.historical_context_summary: Margaret Thatcher delivered this speech during a motion of no confidence brought by the Labour opposition. It was her final major speech in the House of Commons as Prime Minister, having announced her resignation earlier that day.
items.quote_text: Labour's policies are a vote of no confidence in the ability of British people to manage their own affairs. We have that confidence. Confidence in freedom and confidence in enterprise. That is what divides Conservatives from socialists.

items.historical_context_summary: Delivered during the Cold War, Thatcher contrasted the prosperity and freedom of Western capitalist democracies with the failures of communist states. She specifically referenced the Berlin Wall as a physical manifestation of authoritarian coercion.
items.quote_text: Isn't it time we spoke up for our way of life? After all, no Western nation has to build a wall round itself to keep its people in.

items.historical_context_summary: Delivered while she was Leader of the Opposition, Thatcher used this speech to articulate the Conservative Party's philosophical and moral objections to the Labour government's policies.
items.quote_text: The real case against socialism is not its economic inefficiency, though on all sides there is evidence of that. Much more fundamental is its basic immorality.

items.historical_context_summary: Thatcher had recently become Leader of the Conservative Party in 1975. She was addressing her first party conference as leader, outlining her philosophy of individual freedom against the Labour government's socialist policies.
items.quote_text: Every family should have the right to spend their money, after tax, as they wish, and not as the government dictates. Let us extend choice, extend the will to choose and the chance to choose.

items.historical_context_summary: Delivered shortly after Thatcher became Prime Minister in 1979, this speech outlined her philosophy on rolling back the state and restoring individual responsibility. It marked a clear ideological break from the post-war consensus and collectivism.
items.quote_text: If the State usurps or denies the right of the individual to make, where he is able to do so, the important decisions in his life and to provide the essentials for himself and his family, then he is demeaned and diminished as a moral being.

items.historical_context_summary: Delivered shortly after Thatcher's election as Prime Minister in May 1979, following the 'Winter of Discontent'. The UK was experiencing severe economic stagnation, industrial unrest, and a perceived loss of national prestige.
items.quote_text: In the last few years, British patriots have, once again, had cause, as John of Gaunt did, to feel ashamed of the way that the nation was being directed. We know that Britain has been in dire straits before, and that she has recovered. She will recover again.

items.quote_text: Britain is not just another country. We are the country which has always stood at the forefront in defence of freedom. We are the country which stood alone when Europe fell. And we are the country which, for over nine hundred years, has held out against foreign occupation.

items.quote_text: We rejoice that Britain is still respected in all free countries as the Mother of Parliaments and the custodian of the principle of the rule of law.

items.historical_context_summary: During the 1980s, the Labour Party adopted a policy of unilateral nuclear disarmament, promising to cancel the Trident programme. This occurred during a tense period of the Cold War, making nuclear deterrence a central issue in British general elections.
